newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Guam, a paradise island in the Pacific.
newsitem.headline: Guam, a paradise island in the Pacific.

text.p: The island of Guam, an unincorporated territory of the United States in the Pacific Ocean, is a favourite destination of holiday makers from both sides of the ocean.
Approximately 6,500 miles (10,000 km) west from Los Angeles, Guam is nearly 32 miles (50 km) long and varies from four to nine miles (seven to 15 km) wide.
It is the largest and southernmost of the Mariana Islands in the West Pacific.
Its capital Agana is dotted with five-star hotels which offer water sports and outdoor activities. Snorkeling, scuba diving and deep sea fishing are the most popular activities in the island.
Aside from tourism its principal industries include construction, light manufacturing, banking and defence.
Temperature ranges from 21 to 33 degrees Celsius (70 to 90 Fahrenheit) throughout the year.

Guam has a population of some 140,000, of whom 46 percent are indigenous Chamorros, who are basically of Indonesian stock. The rest are made up of Americans from the mainland, Filipinos and Micronesians.
The official languages on the island are Chamorro, which has Spanish roots, and English.
Guam was governed by the U.S. Navy from 1898 to 1941, and from 1944 to 1970, when the people of Guam elected their first civilian governor.

The Spanish explorer Ferdinand Magellan arrived in the Marianas in 1521. Guam, together with the other Mariana Islands, were ceded to the United States in 1898. Spain ruled the Marianas for more than 200 years.
At present, the island hosts the U.S. Andersen Air Force Base and a U.S. Naval Station.
Guamanians became U.S. citizens by virtue of the Organic Act of 1950, and anyone born on Guam since that date is a U.S. citizen.
Guam has a non-voting representative in Washington.
